title: It's The Poverty, Stupid
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene argues that the learning-loss debate keeps avoiding the one factor the evidence points to most strongly: poverty. Citing a Harvard and Stanford analysis reported by the New York Times, he notes that district poverty rates predicted pandemic score drops better than remote learning did. He then walks through decades of reform responses (No Child Left Behind, charters, Teach for America, Race to the Top, vouchers) and argues that each sidestepped poverty while leaning on test prep. The expanded child tax credit briefly cut child poverty to record lows before being dropped, which he reads as proof that we know what works and lack the will. It is a sharp piece of school-policy commentary from Greene's usual vantage.
points: Poverty rate, not school closure alone, was the strongest predictor of pandemic score declines in the Harvard and Stanford district analysis.
Decades of reform have answered poverty with test prep for poor kids at the expense of the full education wealthier kids receive.
The expanded child tax credit cut child poverty to record lows in 2021 and was then allowed to lapse.
Greene's list of reform slogans shows how each fashionable policy relocates the problem onto teachers or individual families instead of addressing poverty itself.
Policy makers prefer a loud learning-loss panic because there is money in it, while the underlying cause gets little attention.
quotes: So remote learning does not explain the whole story. What else does? In a sophisticated analysis of thousands of public school districts in 29 states, researchers at Harvard and Stanford Universities found that poverty played an even bigger role in academic declines during the pandemic.
And after decades, we still don't know a sure-fire way to get poor kids scores up other than subject them to intense test prep at the expense of the rest of the full education that rich kids get
an idea that belongs on the shelf somewhere between trickle-down economics and unicorn farming.

We actually know a good means of reducing child poverty in the US. We just reduced child poverty to record low levels in 2021 by way of expanding the child tax credit plus some other poverty mitigation measures during COVID
Never mind discussing solutions such as a living minimum wage so that working poor can be less poor. Or directing more necessary resources to schools serving poor families.
it will become increasingly clear that A) poverty creates a major hurdle for educational attainment and B) policy makers and thought leaders would much rather talk about something else.
